intro.title: Introduction
intro.lede: Volt UI is a collection of reusable, accessible Angular components built on top of ng-primitives. Inspired by shadcn/ui, you can copy and customize components to match your needs.
intro.aiLede: Volt UI ships with three complementary ways to give AI assistants full context about its components, selectors, and conventions.
intro.skillBody: Auto-discovered by OpenCode / Claude Code. Component catalog, naming, and usage rules.
intro.mcpBody: Hosted MCP tools for listing components, getting examples, and generating CLI commands.
intro.promptBody: A single-file prompt to paste into any LLM chat for correct selectors and examples.
intro.installLede: There are two ways to use Volt UI components in your project:
intro.option1Body: Install the library directly from npm and import components in your project.
intro.option2Body: Copy component source files into your project with ui-* prefix. Full customization.
intro.option3Body: Browse component demos and copy the source code directly. Full control over the implementation.
intro.namingLede: Volt UI uses different prefixes for library source and CLI-generated output.
intro.prereqLede: Before using Volt UI components, ensure you have the following dependencies installed:
intro.npmBody: Runtime dependencies are included automatically. Import the theme CSS once in your global stylesheet.
intro.themeLede: Volt UI provides semantic Tailwind tokens via CSS custom properties. Configure the theme in your app config.
intro.structureLede: When using the CLI, components are added to your project's ui folder:
intro.afterAdding: After adding a component, import and use it in your Angular components:
intro.stableBody: Recommended for production use. Meaningful tests, documented API, and CVA coverage where applicable.
intro.nextThemesBody: Learn how to customize colors, typography, and dark mode.
intro.nextComponentsBody: Explore all available components with examples and source code.
intro.nextAiBody: Configure the MCP server and IDE snippets for Claude, Cursor, Copilot, and more.
intro.cliFlags: Use `--dry-run` to preview files and `--force` to overwrite edited components.
intro.tailwindBody: Volt components ship critical layout CSS, so npm consumers do not need an `@source` directive for `node_modules`.
intro.overlayLede: Dialog, drawer, popover, tooltip, and dropdown-menu use an attribute-directive trigger that references an `<ng-template>` containing the overlay content.
intro.catalogLede: Every component in Volt UI 1.0.0 is **stable** — a settled API, tests that assert the component's own behavior, and documented usage. The **beta** label stays in the system for components added after 1.0; nothing carries it today. See

themesPage.title: Themes
themesPage.lede: Customize the look and feel of your application with built-in themes, colors, and dark mode support.
themesPage.availableLede: Volt UI comes with several pre-built color themes. Each theme provides a unique palette for primary, secondary, accent, and semantic colors.
themesPage.setupLede: Add the theme provider to your application configuration:

styles.brutal: `'brutal'` — No radius, hard offset shadows, heavy borders

themesPage.runtimeLede: Two functions from `@voltui/components` control the theme at runtime. Both just set `data-color`, `data-style` and a `.dark` class on `<html>` — there is no hidden state, so you can inspect or override the result with plain DOM APIs at any time.
themesPage.provideLede: Environment provider. Call it once in `appConfig.providers` to set the theme at bootstrap, on both server and client.
themesPage.provideBody: **SSR-safe.** It reads Angular's `DOCUMENT` injection token rather than the global `document`, so the theme attributes are present in the server-rendered HTML itself — no flash of the default theme while the client bundle hydrates.
themesPage.applyLede: Plain function. Call it from a click handler, an effect, or anywhere else you need to change the theme after bootstrap (e.g. a theme switcher).
themesPage.applyBody: Browser-only by default (it no-ops if `document` is undefined). Pass an explicit `doc` argument to target a different document, e.g. in a test.
themesPage.darkLede: Dark mode is class-based: adding `.dark` to `<html>` switches every component to its dark token values (see `core.css`'s `@custom-variant dark`). Volt does **not** read `prefers-color-scheme` automatically — `dark` defaults to light unless you pass `dark: true` or call `applyVoltTheme` yourself, so the choice is always explicit and won't silently change if the visitor's OS theme changes.
themesPage.varsLede: Every preset sets the same set of semantic tokens as `oklch()` values. Components consume them through Tailwind utilities (`bg-primary`, `text-muted-foreground`) mapped via `@theme inline` in `core.css` — never a raw `var(--primary)`. This is the full list a preset can define; see the two guides below for copy-paste templates.
themesPage.colorPresetLede: A color preset is just a pair of selectors keyed by `data-color`. Copy this template, replace `'mytheme'` and the values, then import the file after `@voltui/components/themes.css` in your global stylesheet.
themesPage.contrastNote: Keep every foreground/background pair at 4.5:1 contrast or better (3:1 for `--ring` and `--input` against `--background`) — see `scripts/contrast-audit.mjs` in the repo for the exact check this project runs against its own presets. The
themesPage.contrastNoteTail: tool generates a starting point from a single accent color if you'd rather not hand-pick eleven tokens.
themesPage.stylePresetLede: A style preset never touches color — only shape. It's keyed by `data-style` and applies to every color at once.
themesPage.styleRegisterNote: Registration is the same as a color preset: put it in your global stylesheet after `@voltui/components/themes.css`, then set `data-style="mystyle"` via `provideVoltTheme` or `applyVoltTheme`.
themesPage.persistNote: The docs app itself persists the visitor's choice to `localStorage` and applies it from a small inline script in `index.html`'s `<head>`, before any stylesheet loads — see `src/app/components/theme-switcher.ts` for a reference implementation if you want the same no-flash behavior client-side.

customizationPage.title: Customization
customizationPage.lede: Every component you add via `npx @voltui/cli add` is copied into your project as plain source. There is no package to eject from and no override API to learn — you edit the file the same way you'd edit any other component you wrote yourself.
customizationPage.editingLede: After `volt add button`, you own `src/app/ui/button/button.ts` (or wherever your CLI config points it). Want a fourth button size? Add it directly — there is nothing else to regenerate or sync.
customizationPage.inferredType: The type `ButtonVariants['size']` is inferred from this object via `VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants>`, so `<volt-button size="xl">` is fully typed the moment you save the file — no separate type declaration to update.
customizationPage.newGroup: Adding a brand-new variant group (not just a new option in an existing one — e.g. a `tone` variant alongside `variant` and `size`) is the same pattern: add the key to `variants` in `variants.ts`, then add `readonly tone = input<...>('default')` and pass it through in the `computed()` above.
customizationPage.cnLede: Most components expose a `class` input that flows through `cn()` — `clsx` for conditional joining, `tailwind-merge` to resolve conflicts so the last utility wins instead of both ending up in the class list:
customizationPage.cnMerge: Because it's `tailwind-merge` underneath, `class="bg-red-500"` reliably overrides the variant's own background utility instead of producing two conflicting `bg-*` classes in the final output.
customizationPage.cvaLedeHead: Components with visual variants (button, badge, toast, ...) split styling into a sibling `variants.ts` using
customizationPage.cvaLedeTail: . The component itself only computes which variant is active — it never hardcodes conditional classes in the template:
customizationPage.colorsLedeHead: Before editing a component's Tailwind classes to change a color or a border-radius, check whether a
customizationPage.colorsLedeTail: already covers it — `bg-primary`, `rounded-md`, and `shadow-lg` all resolve through `--volt-*` tokens that already vary per color/style preset. Hardcoding `bg-indigo-600` in a copied component opts that one component out of theme switching; reach for a custom color or style preset instead when the change should apply everywhere. Component edits are for **structural** changes — new variants, new slots, different markup — that no token could express.

versioningPage.title: Versioning & Stability
versioningPage.lede: Volt UI reached `1.0.0` — the public API is locked and follows ordinary [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/) from here on.
versioningPage.majorBody: The only place breaking changes happen: renamed or removed inputs/outputs/selectors, changed default behavior, dropped Angular major support.
versioningPage.minorBody: New components, new optional inputs/outputs, new CVA variants. Always backward-compatible with the previous minor.
versioningPage.patchBody: Bug fixes, accessibility corrections, internal refactors. Never changes the public contract.
versioningPage.frozenSurface: The frozen surface itself is inventoried in [specs/api-freeze-0.9.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/specs/api-freeze-0.9.md) — every input, output, and selector present at the 1.0.0 freeze. Upgrading from a 0.x release? See [0.x Migration Notes](/docs/migration-notes).
versioningPage.labelsLede: Every component in 1.0.0 is `stable` — see [the component catalog](/docs/components) for the per-component label. `beta` and `experimental` stay defined below because components added after 1.0 may start there; nothing carries either label today. The label is a confidence signal, not an availability gate: every component ships through the npm package and the CLI regardless of label.
versioningPage.stableBody: Recommended for production use. Documented API, meaningful tests, known accessibility caveats (if any) written down.
versioningPage.betaBody: Usable today, but may still gain forms, keyboard, or accessibility hardening in a minor or patch release — that hardening never breaks the existing public API, so moving from beta to stable is a documentation change, not a version bump on its own. Unused in 1.0.
versioningPage.expBody: Reserved for future previews whose API may still change. Not currently used — no shipped component carries this label as of 1.0.0.
versioningPage.angularLede: The `1.x` line targets Angular `^21.2` and Node 20 or newer. Volt UI supports the latest declared Angular major only — widening that range requires consumer-fixture verification, not just a successful build, so it's never assumed.
versioningPage.angularNote: When a new Angular major ships, moving Volt UI's support to it is a minor release with migration notes or release notes documenting anything that changed. A supported major is never dropped silently.
versioningPage.seeAlso: Where the project goes from here: [Roadmap](/docs/roadmap). Full per-component status table: [component catalog](/docs/components). Upgrading an existing copy? [0.x Migration Notes](/docs/migration-notes). Full release history: [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

migrationPage.title: 0.x Migration Notes
migrationPage.lede: Volt UI's public API is frozen as of 1.0.0 — see [Versioning & stability](/docs/versioning) for the current promise. Because components are copied into your project rather than installed as a dependency, "upgrading" means re-running `volt add <component>` (or `--force` to overwrite) and diffing — nothing updates silently underneath you. This page covers the changes across the pre-1.0 `0.x` releases that actually required touching template code when upgrading; see [MIGRATION.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/MIGRATION.md) for the 0.x → 1.0 upgrade guide specifically. Sourced from [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). Most 0.x releases were additive; those aren't listed here.
migrationPage.buttonTypeBody: Before 0.4.0, a `<volt-button>` with no explicit `type` fell through to the browser default inside a `<form>`, which is `"submit"`. If you had a button that relied on that implicit submit behavior, it now does nothing until you set `type="submit"` explicitly.
migrationPage.booleanBody: `disabled`, `required`, `multiple`, and similar boolean inputs across the library switched from plain JS-truthiness checks to Angular's `booleanAttribute` transform. This mainly matters if you were passing a string in a template attribute position — `disabled="false"` as a bare attribute is now correctly treated as `false`, where a naive truthiness check would previously have treated the non-empty string `"false"` as truthy.
migrationPage.additiveLede: These didn't require any change to keep working, but the newer pattern is what current docs and snippets show.
migrationPage.formsTitle: Reactive Forms support added to combobox, listbox, input-OTP
migrationPage.formsBody: These now implement `ControlValueAccessor` in addition to their existing `[(value)]`-style model binding — the old binding still works unchanged. Prefer `formControlName` / `[formControl]` going forward for validation state (`aria-invalid`, disabled propagation, touched) that model binding alone doesn't give you.
migrationPage.selectFix: **0.6.0** `VoltSelect` declared `valueChange` twice; deduplicated so `value = model(...)` owns the single generated output. A normal `(valueChange)` subscriber was never affected.
migrationPage.menuFix: **0.6.0** Keyboard-opened dropdown menus now correctly move focus to the first visible item.
migrationPage.footer: Nothing on this page applies to a component you haven't copied yet — a fresh `volt add` always gives you the current behavior. This page is for diffing an existing copy. See the [Customization guide](/docs/customization) for how to carry your own edits forward across a re-add.

languages.title: Documentation in more languages
languages.summary: The docs are English-only today. Ukrainian (UA) and Spanish (ES) are next, so the library is approachable without reading English first.

details.d1: Applies to this documentation site — guides, component pages, and examples.
details.d2: Component names, selectors, inputs, and outputs stay in English. Translating an API would break every copied component and every code sample on the internet.
details.d3: Language is a reader preference, not a separate build: the same components and the same package back every locale.

headless.title: A first-party headless layer — @volt-ui/core
headless.summary: Replace the ng-primitives dependency with Volt UI’s own headless primitives, so behavior and styling are two layers of one project instead of one project on top of someone else’s.

details.d1: Headless and styled ship separately. Want only the behavior — focus management, keyboard handling, ARIA wiring — with your own markup and CSS? Take @volt-ui/core alone.
details.d2: Want what Volt UI looks like today? Keep using the styled components; they are built on the same headless layer.
details.d3: This happens before the component catalog grows — see the reasoning below.
details.d4: The @volt-ui/core name is already reserved for exactly this in the project spec; it is not a new idea, it is the next one.

distributions.title: Two distributions: with Tailwind and without
distributions.summary: Volt UI is styled with Tailwind CSS v4 today, which rules it out for projects that do not or cannot use Tailwind. A Tailwind-free distribution removes that constraint.

details.d1: The Tailwind build stays the default and keeps working exactly as it does now.
details.d2: The Tailwind-free build ships the same components and the same design tokens as plain CSS.
details.d3: Depends on the headless layer landing first: once behavior is separate from styling, a second styling target stops being a fork and becomes a build output.

layouts.title: More layouts built from Volt UI components
layouts.summary: Beyond the existing sidebar and top-nav layouts — fuller application shells assembled from components that already exist, so a real screen is a starting point rather than an assembly job.

details.d1: Least critical item on this page, and honestly labelled as such — it is a convenience, not a gap.
details.d2: Composed from shipped Volt UI components rather than new one-off primitives.
details.d3: Sequenced last on purpose: layouts built before the headless port would need porting too.

roadmapPage.title: Roadmap
roadmapPage.lede: Volt UI reached `1.0.0`, and 1.0 is a starting line rather than a finish. This is the direction the project is heading and the order it will get there in.
roadmapPage.howToBody: There are no dates here on purpose — a roadmap with dates it can't keep is worse than no roadmap. What is committed is the **order**: each item below depends on the one above it, and shipping them out of sequence would mean redoing work. Anything here that turns out to be wrong gets removed from this page rather than quietly dropped.
roadmapPage.semverNote: None of this breaks your existing code. The 1.0 public API is frozen and everything below follows ordinary semantic versioning — see [Versioning & Stability](/docs/versioning).
roadmapPage.whyTitle: Why the headless layer comes first
roadmapPage.whyBody: The most tempting thing to do after a 1.0 is add components. That is deliberately not what happens next. Every Volt UI component today delegates its accessibility and interaction behavior to [ng-primitives](https://ng-primitives.dev), so every component added before that layer is replaced is one more component to port afterwards. Growing the catalog first would make the migration bigger, slower, and more likely to break your code when it lands.
roadmapPage.whyOrder: Doing it in this order means the port happens once, across the components that exist today, and the catalog grows afterwards on a foundation that is entirely first-party.
roadmapPage.copyInBody: Components stay copyable into your project via the CLI. You own the code you copy; nothing on this page changes that.
roadmapPage.apiBody: Selectors, inputs, and outputs frozen at 1.0 keep working. A breaking change requires a major version and migration notes.
roadmapPage.themingBody: The 5 color × 5 style presets and the token system stay as they are. A Tailwind-free build adds an option; it removes nothing.
roadmapPage.feedback: Have an opinion on the order, or need something that isn't here? Open an issue or a discussion on [GitHub](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui). Shipped work is recorded in [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), and the longer-term technical framing lives in [specs/SPEC.md](https://github.com/Andersseen/volt-ui/blob/main/specs/SPEC.md).

mcpPage.title: AI Integration
mcpPage.lede: Volt UI gives AI assistants three ways to understand and use the component library correctly: a local skill, a hosted MCP server, and a prompt reference.
mcpPage.skillBody: Best for OpenCode / Claude Code users. The skill file is auto-discovered in your workspace and teaches the agent Volt UI conventions, selectors, and the component catalog.
mcpPage.promptBody: Best for web-based LLM chats or agents without MCP/skill support. Paste the contents of `VOLT_UI_PROMPT.md` into any chat for a complete usage guide.
mcpPage.quickStartLede: If you want the fastest path with Claude, Cursor, or Windsurf:
mcpPage.quickStartNote: The installer writes the right config files for your agent and adds Cursor rules / Copilot instructions where applicable.
mcpPage.row1: You use Claude Code or OpenCode
mcpPage.row2: You use Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf
mcpPage.row3: You use GitHub Copilot in VS Code
mcpPage.row4: You use a web chat (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.)
mcpPage.mcpBody: Best for Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, and any MCP-native agent. The hosted server at `{url}` exposes tools to query components, examples, themes, and CLI commands on demand.

aiSkillPage.title: Local Skill
aiSkillPage.lede: A built-in skill file that OpenCode / Claude Code auto-discover in any workspace that uses Volt UI components.
aiSkillPage.whatBody: The skill lives at `.agents/skills/volt-ui/SKILL.md` in the Volt UI repository. Any AI agent that supports OpenCode-style skills will load it automatically and use the conventions, selectors, and component catalog when writing code for your project.
aiSkillPage.installBody: The fastest way to install the skill in a consumer project is to copy it into the standard local-skills location:
aiSkillPage.coversStack: **Stack context** — Angular 21, zoneless signals, OnPush, standalone, Tailwind v4, ng-primitives, CVA
aiSkillPage.coversNaming: **Naming conventions** — `ui-*` vs `volt-*`, element vs attribute selectors
aiSkillPage.coversCatalog: **Component catalog** — stable and beta components with selectors and key inputs
aiSkillPage.coversOverlays: **Overlay rules** — attribute-directive triggers + `<ng-template>` for dialog, drawer, popover, tooltip, dropdown-menu
aiSkillPage.coversForms: **Reactive Forms** — which components are CVA and how to wire `FormControl`
aiSkillPage.coversTheme: **Theme system** — `provideVoltTheme`, colors, styles, and dark mode
aiSkillPage.exampleBody: The skill explicitly tells the agent never to write `<ui-dialog>`, `<ui-tooltip>`, or other invalid element selectors.

aiPromptPage.title: Prompt Reference
aiPromptPage.lede: A single-file prompt you can paste into any LLM chat to get correct selectors, examples, and rules for Volt UI components.
aiPromptPage.whatBody: `VOLT_UI_PROMPT.md` is a self-contained prompt reference. It tells the LLM everything it needs to know about Volt UI: installation, naming, the full component catalog, overlay rules, Reactive Forms examples, and troubleshooting.
aiPromptPage.copyLede: Paste the contents below at the top of a new chat with any LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Cursor Chat, etc.), then ask your question.
aiPromptPage.howStep2: Paste it at the top of a new chat with your LLM.
aiPromptPage.howStep3: Ask your question, e.g. "Create a login form with Volt UI components."
aiPromptPage.insideCatalog: **Component catalog** — stable and beta components with selectors and notes
aiPromptPage.insideOverlays: **Overlay rules** — dialog, drawer, popover, tooltip, dropdown-menu templates
aiPromptPage.insideRules: **AI assistant rules** — what to do and what not to do when generating Volt UI code
aiPromptPage.whenBody: Use the prompt reference when your editor or agent doesn't support MCP or local skills yet. It's also handy for one-off questions in web-based LLM chats.
aiPromptPage.whenAlt: For integrated agents, prefer the [MCP server](/docs/ai-mcp) or the [local skill](/docs/ai-skill) so the context stays in sync automatically.

aiMcpPage.title: MCP Server
aiMcpPage.lede: A hosted Model Context Protocol server that exposes Volt UI components, usage examples, theme info, and CLI commands as tools any compatible agent can call.
aiMcpPage.setupLede: Run the interactive installer from your project directory:
aiMcpPage.setupNote: It asks which agent(s) to set up, then writes the right config files automatically. You can also pass the agent directly:
aiMcpPage.claudeBody: Claude Desktop and Claude Code — full tool access via the hosted MCP server.
aiMcpPage.claudeWrites: Writes `.claude/mcp.json` and patches the Claude Desktop global config if found.
aiMcpPage.cursorBody: Full MCP support plus a `.cursorrules` file with component context for inline suggestions.
aiMcpPage.windsurfBody: Codeium's Windsurf editor with native MCP support.
aiMcpPage.copilotBody: Copilot doesn't support MCP HTTP yet — the installer writes a Copilot instructions file and VS Code snippets instead.
aiMcpPage.manualLede: For MCP-native agents, add this entry to your config file:
aiMcpPage.learnsComponents: **All components** — 41 components across stable and beta status labels
aiMcpPage.learnsSelectors: **Correct selectors** — element components vs attribute directives for overlays
aiMcpPage.learnsVariants: **Variants & inputs** — solid, outline, ghost, destructive + sizes
aiMcpPage.learnsPrompts: **Reusable prompts** — component generation and troubleshooting prompts
aiMcpPage.examplesLede: After setup, try asking your AI assistant:
aiMcpPage.apiBody: The server implements the MCP Streamable HTTP transport. It is stateless and returns JSON responses for POST requests.
aiMcpPage.whatBody: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets LLMs talk to external tools, resources, and prompts. The Volt UI MCP server runs at `{url}` and exposes a spec-compliant Streamable HTTP endpoint. Agents can list components, read detailed metadata, fetch usage examples, and even retrieve reusable prompts.
aiMcpPage.discoveryNote: `GET {url}` returns human-readable discovery JSON (tools, resources, prompts, setup links).

skeleton.title: Skeleton
skeleton.description: Use to show a placeholder while content is loading.

slider.title: Slider
slider.description: An input where the user selects a value from within a given range.

switch.title: Switch
switch.description: A control that allows the user to toggle between checked and not checked.

table.title: Table
table.description: A responsive table component for displaying tabular data.

tabs.title: Tabs

toggle.title: Toggle
toggle.description: A two-state button that can be either on or off.

tooltip.title: Tooltip
tooltip.description: A popup that displays information related to an element when the element receives keyboard focus or the mouse hovers over it.

autofill.title: Autofill
autofill.description: Directive for detecting browser autofill state on form controls.

combobox.title: Combobox
combobox.description: Searchable select input with a custom option template.

datePicker.title: Date Picker
datePicker.description: Calendar primitives for date and range selection.

fileUpload.title: File Upload
fileUpload.description: File picker trigger and drag-and-drop dropzone primitives.

formField.description: Accessible form wrapper with label, hint, and error text.

index.title: Components

inputOtp.description: One-time password input for verification and PIN flows.

listbox.title: Listbox

pagination.title: Pagination

search.title: Search

textarea.title: Textarea

toast.title: Toast

toggleGroup.title: Toggle Group

toolbar.title: Toolbar

catalog.orBrowse: or browse below to copy source code.

hero.label: Hero
hero.blurb: The first screen. What the product is, and the one thing to do about it.

features.label: Features
features.blurb: What it does, arranged so the important one is visibly the important one.

services.label: Services
services.blurb: What you do for someone, when the product is a team rather than a download.

proof.label: Social proof
proof.blurb: Other people saying it, which is the only version anyone believes.

pricing.label: Pricing
pricing.blurb: Plans, the difference between them, and the one you would like picked.

contact.label: Contact
contact.blurb: A form that works, next to the ways of reaching you that are not a form.

cta.label: Call to action
cta.blurb: The last chance to convert someone who read the whole page.

footer.label: Footer
footer.blurb: The sitemap, the legal bits, and the newsletter nobody scrolls back up for.

auth.label: Auth
auth.blurb: Screens where the page is the component. The layouts tab has the same ones stripped to their skeleton.

app.label: Application
app.blurb: The screens behind the login, with the work done rather than left as slots.

hero.label: Hero Spotlight
hero.tagline: Centred opening with a spotlight that follows the pointer.
hero.motion: A radial spotlight tracks the pointer, two auroras drift behind the grid, the headline word shimmers, and the content rises in five steps at first paint.

heroSplit.label: Hero Split
heroSplit.tagline: Copy on the left, a live product panel on the right, tilted toward the reader.
heroSplit.motion: The panel sits on a slight 3D tilt that straightens as the pointer approaches, and a status row ticks through states on its own.

bento.label: Feature Bento
bento.tagline: Asymmetric grid where each card lights its own border under the cursor.
bento.motion: Each card carries a radial fill and a one-pixel gradient ring that follow the pointer inside that card, plus a lift on hover.

services.label: Service List
services.tagline: Numbered rows that open as you point at them, instead of four equal cards.
services.motion: The row under the pointer expands to reveal its detail and deliverables while the others recede, so the section reads as one thing at a time.

testimonials.label: Testimonial Marquee
testimonials.tagline: Two rows of quotes sliding in opposite directions, pausing under the pointer.
testimonials.motion: Each row loops a duplicated list by exactly half its width, so the seam is invisible, and stops on hover or focus.

pricing.label: Pricing Tiers
pricing.tagline: Three plans with an annual switch, animated prices and a scaled featured tier.
pricing.motion: Switching the billing period replays the price entrance, the savings badge slides in, and the featured tier sits scaled above the row.

contact.label: Contact Split
contact.tagline: A real form beside the ways of reaching you that are not a form.
contact.motion: Each field group grows an accent bar and brightens its label on focus, and submitting swaps the form for a confirmation in place, with focus moved onto it.

cta.label: Magnetic CTA
cta.tagline: Closing panel with a rotating gradient border and a button that leans toward you.
cta.motion: A conic gradient spins around the panel edge, and the submit button is pulled toward the pointer while it is within 140px.

login.label: Login Split
login.tagline: A marketing panel beside the form — the shipped version of the login layout.
login.motion: Two auroras drift behind the brand panel, and the copy and form rise in three steps at first paint. The panel itself is dropped, not stacked, once the section is too narrow for it.

footer.label: Footer Sitemap
footer.tagline: Four link columns, a newsletter field, and a status line that is actually live.
footer.motion: Column links slide their underline out from the left on hover, and the status dot pulses on a slow loop.

dashboard.label: Dashboard
dashboard.tagline: Branded shell, figures that count up, and a chart that draws itself.
dashboard.motion: The figures count to their value the first time the row is scrolled into view, once and never again, and the chart strokes itself on as it arrives. Both start finished under reduced motion.

logoCloud.label: Logo Cloud
logoCloud.tagline: Customer logos that settle into place as the section arrives.

faq.label: FAQ
faq.tagline: Accordion built on the accessible primitive, with a search field over it.

stats.label: Stats
stats.tagline: Figures that count up once, the first time they are scrolled into view.

team.label: Team
team.tagline: Portraits that swap for a role and a link when you point at them.

adminDashboard.label: Admin Dashboard
adminDashboard.tagline: Collapsible sidebar, top bar, and a content area with stats and a table.
adminDashboard.structure: A sidebar that collapses to icons, a top bar carrying the collapse control and a breadcrumb, and a scrolling content area. The stat row and table are there to show what the content area is for — they are the part you replace.

topNav.label: Top Navigation
topNav.tagline: Horizontal navigation instead of a sidebar, for apps with few sections.
topNav.structure: A full-width header holding the brand, the primary navigation and the account menu, over a centred content column. The shape to reach for when the sections fit on one line.

analytics.label: Analytics
analytics.tagline: A metrics page: filter bar, KPI row, and panels sized by importance.
analytics.structure: A filter bar pinned above a KPI row, then a grid where the panels are deliberately unequal — the chart is worth more space than the list beside it.

sidebar.label: Sidebar
sidebar.tagline: The sidebar component itself: API, collapse behaviour and width control.
sidebar.structure: Unlike the rest of this tab, this documents a component that ships in the library rather than an arrangement you copy. The layouts above are built on it.

settings.label: Settings
settings.tagline: Section navigation beside a form column, the shape every settings page has.
settings.structure: A narrow list of sections on the left and one form column on the right, with each group separated rather than boxed. Scales to more sections without redesigning anything.

profile.label: Profile
profile.tagline: An identity header over tabbed detail panels.
profile.structure: A header carrying who this is and the actions you can take on them, then tabs for the detail. The header stays put while the tabs change what is underneath.

kanban.label: Kanban Board
kanban.tagline: Columns that scroll horizontally with cards that scroll inside them.
kanban.structure: The two-axis scrolling problem, solved: the board scrolls sideways, each column scrolls its own cards, and neither one steals the other gesture.

chat.label: Chat
chat.tagline: A conversation list, a message thread, and a composer pinned to the bottom.
chat.structure: Three regions with different scroll behaviour: the list scrolls, the thread scrolls and starts at the bottom, and the composer never moves.

login.label: Login
login.tagline: A centred credential form with the fields wired to form-field.
login.structure: One card, centred on both axes, with labels bound to their inputs and hints in the slot that announces them. Deliberately unbranded — the blocks gallery is where a login gets a face.

signUp.label: Sign Up
signUp.tagline: Registration with validation slots and the terms checkbox that gates submit.
signUp.structure: The login shape plus what registration adds: more fields, a place for per-field errors, and a submit that stays disabled until the terms are accepted.
